source.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
source.authors: S. Reddy; Amro Abbas; Anshuman Suri; Ari S. Morcos; David Schwab; Pratyush Maini

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses emergent misalignment as a setting for developing and validating gradient attribution, then applies that approach to safety filtering. Its reported gradient-similarity and filtering results do not measure the unrelated free-form misaligned-answer rates named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The emergent-misalignment experiments report gradient-similarity AUCs, not rates of harmful answers. The SafeTulu experiments report jailbreak ASRs after filtering a broad instruction dataset, not after the narrow-task, inoculation, or brief-retraining interventions named by the versions. These results are recorded as findings about related constructs under fits_no_version. The embedding-cost/math AUC ablations and capability benchmark results are not rows because they do not measure the claim's predicted behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper treats insecure-code emergent misalignment as given. It uses existing misaligned checkpoints (Betley Qwen-Coder-Insecure and a Mistral-24B reproduction) to validate a gradient-attribution method. It reports only gradient-similarity ROC-AUCs separating insecure from secure training code. It never reports rates of misaligned free-form answers, versus a base model or matched controls. The SafeTulu part measures jailbreak attack success rates after filtering a broad dataset (Tulu 3). That is a different construct from emergent misalignment, and no narrow-task, inoculation, or benign-retraining intervention is involved.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude that in emergently misaligned models, insecure-code gradients align with the emergent harmful outputs (AUC up to 0.865), and that this signal is absent before fine-tuning. They conclude that SimpleLoRIF-built SafeTulu cuts GCG ASR by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama and Olmo while largely preserving capability, outperforming judge and He et al. filtering. They do not measure emergent-misalignment rates.
record.recipe_differences: The EM analysis uses existing insecure-code fine-tuned checkpoints and matched source datasets to measure gradient-similarity AUC, rather than reproducing the behavioral-rate comparison. SafeTulu separately filters a broad instruction dataset and fine-tunes models on the retained data.
record.method_sensitivity: The gradient signal varies by embedding model and target-response model: cross-model transfer is strong in one direction and sharply lower in the other. In non-misaligned Qwen2.5-Coder models, AUC rises through 14B and falls at 32B. SafeTulu removal-fraction results also vary: on Llama 3.2 1B, gradient filtering helps through 20% removal but ASR rises at 40%.

fits_no_version.finding: In insecure-code fine-tuned checkpoints, insecure examples are more gradient-similar than matched secure examples to the model's own misaligned outputs: AUC 0.865 for Mistral, 0.604 for Qwen. Base models score 0.431 and 0.552.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment leaves a training-data-attribution footprint. After fine-tuning, insecure-code examples' gradients align with gradients of unrelated harmful outputs; before fine-tuning they do not.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-family transfer of this gradient signal is asymmetric: 0.865→0.832 for the Mistral embedder, but 0.604→0.247 for the Qwen embedder. Base-model transfer is near chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gradient footprint of emergent misalignment depends on the embedding model and target-model pairing.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient AUC in non-misaligned Qwen2.5-Coder models rises from 0.5B to 14B (0.507→0.590), then falls at 32B (0.552).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size of the attribution signal is non-monotonic in model scale. This says nothing about the rate of misaligned behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the 20% of Tulu 3 most gradient-aligned with unsafe SafeRLHF responses lowers GCG and ActorBreaker ASR across four models. This beats judge filtering and He et al., and the benefit reverses at 40% removal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-based filtering of benign instruction data reduces fine-tuning-induced jailbreak vulnerability. This is safety degradation, not emergent misalignment.

record.problems: The EM experiment reports gradient-similarity AUC rather than harmful-answer rates. The paper states that cross-model gradient representations may not transfer, and the scaling AUC trend is non-monotonic. SafeTulu is evaluated against two jailbreak attacks and one target set; the authors state they do not test other target sets or specific harms such as sycophancy. SafeTulu attack rates are reported over three seeds as mean ± one standard error.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected claim-relevant results. The paper's embedding-cost/math-benchmark ablations and capability scores are excluded because they do not measure the claim's predicted behavior. The claim-version verdicts remain not_tested because the included results measure gradient similarity or responses to jailbreak attacks under a different training intervention.

untested.parts: No rate of misaligned free-form answers after insecure-code fine-tuning. No secure-code or educational-insecure fine-tuned controls evaluated behaviourally. Misaligned responses were collected only to serve as gradient targets.
No other narrow fine-tunes (medical, financial, reward hacks, numbers).
No linear direction or persona feature examined. Gradient similarity between training data and outputs is a different construct.
No inoculation or brief benign re-training. Data filtering is applied only to Tulu 3 and evaluated with jailbreak ASR, not emergent-misalignment rates.
No effect size, seed robustness, coherence filtering or training-time emergence of the misaligned behaviour. The scaling sweep is gradient AUC in non-misaligned models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4 / uses_without_test call is right. All rows correctly carry versions none. Main fixes are subject labels on the fine-tuned EM rows and the duplicate R04/R13. The text's Table 8 caption ('smaller models may have a sharper gradient signal') conflicts with its own numbers; this has no bearing on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure rates of unrelated misaligned free-form answers after insecure-code fine-tuning against the base model and matched secure-code and educational-insecure-code controls.
No fine-tunes on bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences are tested for spontaneous unrelated misalignment.
No narrow in-context examples are tested for spontaneous unrelated misalignment.
No reinforcement-learning intervention, including learned reward hacks, is tested for spontaneous unrelated misalignment.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is tested as a mediator across fine-tunes.
The study filters training data; it does not test framing bad behavior as requested during training or brief benign retraining.
The scaling sweep measures gradient-similarity AUC in non-misaligned models, not the size or robustness of the misalignment behavior across seeds, coherence filters, or training stages.
